articles.title: Lessons for YDSA from Serbia’s Mass Protests
articles.content: This article was written in the lead-up to the recent YDSA National Convention in Chicago to motivate the passage of “Resolution 9: For a Strategic Sanctuary Campaign on All Fronts.” The resolution has since passed and two R&R members, Kaeden Boudreaux and Tomas Jimenez, were elected as at-large members of the YDSA National Coordinating Committee on a party-building, class-struggle, mass politics platform. On June 27, Serbia’s President Aleksandar Vučić announced he would resign “within weeks.” This was in response to the largest protest wave since the movement which overthrew the dictator Slobodan Milošević in 2000. No date was set. No election was actually called. The same weekend, Vučić was already hinting he would return as the prime minister, a job he held from 2014 to 2017. Despite frequent derision as an anti-democratic strongman, the Serbian president holds very limited legal power under Serbia’s parliamentary constitution. Vučić’s real power runs through the vast patronage machine of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which he formally led from 2012 to 2023 and still dominates, and which has controlled parliament for the last decade. Serbian analysts read the move as another tactical maneuver to relieve public pressure without touching SNS’s actual grip on the state. The protesters weren’t fooled. The next morning in Kraljevo they said as much, doubting Vučić’s resignation would amount to real change, and have since taken to the streets in even greater numbers. It’s worth asking why they weren’t fooled. In May 2026, the month before his announcement, Vučić traveled to Beijing . Along with some great interview clips , he received China’s Friendship Medal and signed a memorandum joining China’s Global Security Initiative, an explicit alternative to NATO and the EU security frameworks, alongside new deals for Chinese air defense systems and combat drones. Serbia has long played the great powers against each other. In this century, they’ve been dependent on Russia for energy and their claims on Kosovo, the EU for trade (especially by exporting lithium ), and now simultaneously deepening security ties with China and the USA . Managing the great powers, the “four pillars” , is one of the SNS’s most durable sources of legitimacy. This all means that the nation’s President can announce he’s resigning while all of that, the one-party patronage machine, the security deals, the great-power hedging which maintains their exports and energy, stays exactly in place. That’s the concession Serbian students have won, a real political victory, but nowhere near enough. This is the same trap every YDSA sanctuary campus is at risk of falling into, and it’s the reason our caucus Reform & Revolution is backing Resolution 9: For a Strategic Sanctuary Campaign on All Fronts . A university administration can announce a commission, a statement of values supporting immigrants, promise you personally that they’ll “look into it,” and lose nothing that actually matters, the same way Vučić can announce his resignation and SNS loses nothing that actually matters. The lesson is, don’t let your target symbolically concede, keep fighting for the substance of your program. The protests didn’t start as a fight over Vučić at all. On November 1, 2024, a concrete canopy at the Novi Sad railway station collapsed onto the platform below, killing sixteen people waiting for their train. The canopy had been “renovated” twice in two years under a Chinese-Hungarian infrastructure consortium funded by Belt and Road contracts. Later investigation revealed the records for these renovations were incomplete, contradictory, and in places missing entirely, even after months of digging. It was a perfect symbol for the decade of SNS rule defined by corruption in public contracting. The slogan that emerged, “We are all under the canopy,” was less about the train station, more a rejection of the cronyism of Serbia’s government. The early protests were characterized by mourning . Silent vigils, disorganized demonstrations at Novi Sad city hall and at universities, a culture war waged in the media, a few cabinet resignations, and virulent right-wing attacks on protesters. By December, classes were suspended at most university campuses and a number of high schools as physical blockades took hold for days and weeks on end. By January the nation had become severely polarized, with the protests spreading to every city and campus and right-wing violence intensifying, often backed physically by Serbian police and rhetorically by SNS politicians. The state’s response to scrutiny followed a familiar global pattern. When a mysterious blast of sound sent hundreds of protesters into a panicked stampede at a March 2025 rally, breaking one protestor’s leg and sending hundreds more to seek medical treatment, Serbia’s police and army fiercely denied possessing an acoustic weapon. Confronted with photos of the devices, the California -made Genasys 450 XLR and LRAD 100X sonic weapons, officials admitted purchasing them but insisted they were never used, calling them “loudspeakers” available on eBay. Serbian rights groups have since taken the matter to the European Court of Human Rights with over 4,000 testimonies. It’s the same instinct as the resignation announcement a year later, to offer a technically defensible non-answer, and hope the public moves on before anyone can check. In January, with the backing of 60 percent of the public and the public sector and education unions, protesters began to consolidate around four demands that have driven the movement since: Publication of all documents relating to the Novi Sad railway station renovation Filing criminal charges against those who attacked protesters Dismissal of charges against all arrested and detained students, activists, and citizens A 20 percent increase in the university system budget None of that required agreeing on an entire theory of Serbian politics. They name a specific document, specific set of assailants, specific set of political prisoners, and a specific budget line. That’s the difference between a demand that a target – whether an Eastern European strongman or a public university president – can be forced to answer, and a demand they can wait out. You cannot “process” a request to publish specific documents the way you can process a call for “change.” You either publish them or you visibly refuse to, and either way, the state has moved onto the students’ terrain instead of its own. R9 is built exactly on this logic. Rather than asking universities to affirm a “sanctuary campus” as a value (something outlawed in many Republican states), it names Palantir, Flock Safety, Elbit Systems, Oracle, OpenAI, and demands their contracts be cut. It names 287(g) agreements and demands they be revoked. It names a ban on ICE and DHS recruitment. Every one of those is as checkable as the renovation documents. The blockades weren’t just walkouts and statements read to a crowd. Once students occupied their departments, they opened up plenums, these are public assemblies open to any student, deliberating on the movement’s next moves. No student union or student government bureaucracy filtered the agenda. No self-appointed spokespeople negotiated on anyone’s behalf. Instead the students who occupied the building governed it through daily, sometimes hours-long meetings. This wasn’t invented from nothing, Serbian universities have a long history of plenums , drawing on socialist Yugoslavia’s own tradition of workplace self-management. The protesters are in effect reviving this form now, against a government that has spent a decade hollowing out every remaining democratic institution in the country (such as by owning or influencing over 90 percent of media ). Over time, the plenums did far more than deliberate . Working groups split off to handle finances, communications, security, and relationships with unions and sympathetic faculty. Over the course of 2025 these national structures matured enough that a decision voted on in Belgrade could be echoed, debated, and adapted in Novi Sad or Niš the same day. Occupied university buildings stopped being where students used to attend lectures and became something closer to a distributed institution, a place to deliberate, organize, and escalate as a collective. That fusion of real bottom-up legitimacy fused to a real capacity for disruption is the easiest part of this movement to admire and hardest to copy. It’s also the exact gap in a lot of American campus organizing, which too often treats democracy and action as contradictory priorities rather than the same muscle. YDSA has begun to bridge this gap with its cohort structure, where chapters with similar campaigns targeting 287(g) agreements or the same corporations share research and pressure tactics. R9 continues and formalizes these practices piloted last year, fusing our organizing capacity across the country so that university administration cannot pick off our chapter’s demands one-by-one the way Vučić is betting he can wait out this symbolic resignation. The movement itself never resolved what it actually was, and mostly refused to try. From the first plenums, students deliberately kept the protests non-partisan, framing themselves as representing “all Serbians” rather than any single political current. This makes sense given decades of the Vučić regime’s successfully discrediting opposition parties as corrupt or foreign-controlled, and it’s one that let the movement pull in liberals, conservatives, socialists, populists, and the apolitical under one roof. That same universalist framing is also why the movement was never going to be socialist, or anything else with a class program: it was built, on purpose, to be a vessel broad enough that almost no one in Serbian society could say it wasn’t theirs. The movement’s own universalist “we represent all Serbians” framing has meant it can’t exclude those to the right of the SNS government too. Journalist Vincent Bevins, reporting from inside the protests for the London Review of Books , documented far-right speakers at a Kosovo commemoration rally within the movement’s orbit. Orthodox nationalist speakers, motivated by grievances separate from corruption and education, have been able to ride the movement’s credibility into their own influence. The movement’s organizers seem uneasy about this, without a clean answer. Serbia’s organized left is very small and fragmented, and didn’t agree on how to treat any of this. Some of the country’s Trotskyist and Marxist-Leninist formations stayed on the sidelines, arguing the movement “lacks a class character,” that a protest movement backed by neoliberal opposition figures and establishment unions, without a socialist program, wasn’t a fight worth joining. Reporting and analysis from our own tradition’s international network, the CWI, has treated that abstention as a real failure. They wrote that a left that only shows up if a movement arrives pre-packaged with the right politics abandons the actual task of the left, which is to offer direction inside movements while consciousness is still forming, not after. Two other forces on the Serbian left took a different approach. The Green–Left Front (ZLF), Serbia’s largest party to the left of SNS, backed the protests’ demands from its position in the opposition and has consistently allied with them at public rallies. The Party of the Radical Left (PRL), a smaller socialist group with no parliamentary seats but real credibility inside the movement, took the more instructive approach for YDSA. It didn’t claim to have organized the blockades, defended the plenum’s self-organization, and pushed back on the state’s claims. PRL also warned – more than once – that a premature turn toward electoral politics would trade the plenums’ direct democracy for a seat at the negotiating table, the same seat every co-opted Balkan opposition party has taken before. It’s tempting, observing from the outside, to resolve that ambiguity by picking a side. To decide the movement is, or decide it’s compromised beyond use, and stop thinking about it either way. PRL’s approach shows why both are mistakes. A movement doesn’t have to already be socialist for socialists to have real, unfinished work to do inside it, arguing for its best instincts against its worst ones without ever pretending to speak for the majority. That’s the same relationship socialists have to the growing anti-ICE sentiments of the US population , “anti-ICE” is a movement we didn’t start and don’t control. A concession that doesn’t touch the actual machinery of power isn’t unique to Vučić. It’s exactly what university administrations offer every time “sanctuary campus” moves through sympathetic statements and committee hearings rather than policy, while every actual point of contact between the university and ICE stays. That’s the gap our own 2025-2026 Sanctuary Campus Campaigns have run into in many cases. Real chapter capacity has been built, often membership doubled or tripled, but broad demands let administrations offer performative wins instead of material ones, and the campaign’s energy slowly fizzled away. R9 exists to close that gap for the 2026-2027 school year, and closes it the way Novi Sad’s students did, by naming the specific things that have to change. It asks universities to: Terminate any 287(g) agreement between campus police and ICE Bar ICE agents from campus without a judicial warrant Prohibit ICE and DHS recruitment on university grounds Cut contracts and procurement ties with the corporations building the deportation and surveillance infrastructure ICE runs on: Palantir, Flock Safety, Elbit, Oracle, and OpenAI Sever investment, research, and recruitment pipelines into the military and police Every one of those is concrete. A university either has a 287(g) agreement, or it doesn’t. It either has a contract with OpenAI and Palantir, or it doesn’t. Just like the canopy documents, there’s no room for a university to “process” a way out of the answer, it either cuts the tie, visibly refuses to. Either way, the fight moves onto favorable terrain the administration doesn’t control. None of this happens through moral pressure alone. Serbia’s students didn’t win what they’ve won that way either. It took blockades that shut down normal university operations, strikes across the education system and major sectors, plenums that gave the blockades democratic legitimacy and staying power, and coordination across dozens of campuses so that no single administration or city government could simply wait out one isolated group of students. That coordination is exactly what R9’s organizing cohorts are built to provide nationally, on a realistic timeline, rather than 128 separate chapters running 128 separate campaigns. Serbian students haven’t won yet. Vučić is still in power, still hedging between Washington, Brussels, Moscow, and Beijing, and the plenums know it, which is why they’re still in the streets instead of declaring victory and going home. A parliamentary poll in June found that , while SNS still leads with 47 percent of decided voters, that the newly founded Student List is now Serbia’s clear second-largest political force, trailing SNS by only sixteen points. Although Vučić’s governing coalition has majority support combined with their ally the Socialist Party of Serbia, the fact the student protesters have unified Serbia’s opposition is a serious achievement, won by years of organizing. Power is not granted. It has to be organized, demand by demand, campus by campus, workplace by workplace, until the people who run these institutions have no room left to wait us out. YDSA delegates should adopt R9, and every chapter should be ready to join a Strategic Campaign Committee cohort next semester, to struggle for freedom as one united force as the brave students in Serbia are doing.

articles.title: Veterans, Labor, and the Fight to Save the VA From Privatization
articles.author: Steve Early
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. At a time when federal workers face mounting attacks on their jobs, collective bargaining rights, and public services, a growing coalition of veterans and labor activists is working to defend one of America's most important public institutions: the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA). That struggle was the focus of How Veterans in Labor Are Fighting Trump, VA Privatization, & Union Busting , a discussion at the 4th Annual Left Coast Forum, held October 2–4, 2026, at Cal State LA. The session featured Eric Goepel , an Army veteran, Communications Workers of America (CWA) Local 6251 member, and Southern California organizer for Common Defense, a progressive veterans organization. Steve Early , longtime labor journalist, union activist, and co-author of Courage or Complicity: How Veterans Are Responding to the Attack on Democracy , moderated the discussion. Their central argument was that veterans possess an often-overlooked source of political power: their presence within organized labor and their capacity to mobilize across traditional political divisions. Veterans in Labor Are Fighting Trump (1:07:32) Veterans Are an Untapped Force in Organized Labor Early emphasized that approximately one million former military service members belong to labor unions, yet relatively few unions systematically identify, organize, or develop these members as activists. He argued that unions have historically underestimated veterans' potential as organizers, even though military veterans have played important roles in some of America's most consequential labor struggles. From the Teamsters' reform movement to battles against corrupt union leadership, veterans have repeatedly demonstrated their willingness to challenge powerful institutions. Early suggested that unions should establish networks of veteran shop stewards, local officers, and rank-and-file members, providing political education and leadership training that connects workplace struggles with broader campaigns for social justice. Goepel agreed, describing veteran organizing as a potential "force multiplier." When veterans receive training and opportunities to organize within their existing communities, their influence can extend far beyond individual membership. With millions of workers represented by AFL-CIO unions, the organizational infrastructure already exists to make veteran activism a significant force within the labor movement. The missing ingredient, both speakers suggested, is sustained commitment. Related: ICE Killing in Maine Shows Why Vets Need Vetting—And Not Just in Politics The Fight Against VA Privatization Goepel described Common Defense's campaign, "VA Not for Sale," which challenges the growing diversion of veterans' healthcare funding into private medical systems. Over the past two decades, federal policies have increasingly expanded the use of private-sector providers through the VA's community care programs. Goepel argued that these policies threaten to weaken the public healthcare system by transferring resources away from VA facilities already struggling with staffing shortages. But the problem reaches beyond veterans. The VA is also a major training institution for America's healthcare workforce. Physicians, nurses, medical researchers, and other professionals gain valuable experience through its hospitals and affiliated medical centers. Weakening the VA, Goepel argued, therefore threatens the broader healthcare system. His proposed response involves restoring staffing, rebuilding institutional capacity, and reversing policies that encourage privatization rather than strengthening public services. The objective is not simply preserving existing programs. It is demonstrating that publicly provided healthcare can deliver high-quality services without making private profits its organizing principle. Why Veterans' Benefits Should Inform Healthcare for Everyone One of Goepel's most significant observations concerned the contradiction between America's treatment of veterans and its treatment of the broader population. Veterans have access to a network of public benefits involving healthcare, education, housing assistance, disability compensation, and employment support. Although these systems have serious shortcomings and inequalities, Goepel argued that they demonstrate something important: government can establish comprehensive programs intended to meet essential human needs. Why, he asked, should comparable protections remain unavailable to millions of other Americans? He pointed to military toxic exposure as another example. Veterans harmed by burn pits and other hazardous conditions have won expanded recognition and benefits through federal legislation. Yet civilians living near contaminated military installations may face similar environmental consequences without equivalent protections. For Goepel, defending veterans' benefits and expanding social rights are not competing objectives. They are connected struggles. Related: Not Every Veteran Candidate Is a Champion for Veterans Confronting the Military-Industrial Complex The discussion eventually moved beyond VA privatization to the enormous federal resources devoted to military spending. Participants questioned why Washington continues expanding military budgets while threatening cuts to healthcare, education, housing, and other public services. Goepel acknowledged a difficult contradiction: military contracting supports many well-paying union jobs. Workers employed by defense contractors cannot reasonably be expected to embrace reductions in weapons production without credible alternatives for their livelihoods. Early pointed to the concept of economic conversion , an approach advocated by labor reformers for decades. Rather than simply eliminating military production jobs, economic conversion would redirect industrial capacity toward civilian needs while protecting workers' wages, benefits, and employment opportunities. Factories producing military equipment, for example, could be redirected toward infrastructure, public transportation, or other socially useful production. Both speakers argued that such a transition requires government investment and planning, not abandonment of affected workers. The issue is ultimately one of national priorities: whether public resources should continue sustaining an expanding weapons industry or be redirected toward meeting human needs. Building Solidarity Beyond Veterans' Organizations The panel also examined differences between traditional veterans' service organizations and newer advocacy groups such as Common Defense. Organizations including the American Legion and Veterans of Foreign Wars have historically played important roles in securing benefits and helping veterans navigate complicated claims processes. But traditional organizations have often avoided more confrontational political advocacy. Common Defense operates through nonprofit and political structures that allow it to participate more directly in campaigns, elections, and public policy debates. Goepel argued that veterans' credibility across political and geographic divisions gives them an unusual opportunity to communicate with communities that progressive organizations sometimes struggle to reach. That credibility, however, must be used to build solidarity rather than simply advance the interests of veterans alone. Related: When Workplace Organizing Gets Tough, Here’s How to Keep Going From Defending Institutions to Building Collective Power The larger message emerging from the Left Coast Forum discussion was that defending the VA cannot be separated from defending organized labor, public healthcare, and democratic accountability. The attacks on federal workers, the privatization of essential services, and the concentration of economic power are interconnected. So must be the response. Early and Goepel offered a vision of veterans not merely as recipients of government benefits or symbols of military service, but as workers, organizers, and advocates capable of helping build a broader movement. Their challenge to organized labor was equally clear: stop overlooking the veterans already within union ranks. And their challenge to the country was more ambitious. If Americans can establish public institutions to provide healthcare, education, and economic security for those who served in uniform, why should those same commitments to human dignity remain beyond reach for everyone else?

articles.title: Statement in Solidarity with Ilhan Omar
articles.author: Metro DC DSA
articles.content: Statement in Solidarity with Ilhan Omar Date: October 14, 2026 Media Contact: For all press inquiries, please contact media@mdcdsa.org . Washington, DC: Metro DC DSA condemns in the strongest possible terms the Trump administration’s raid on Ilhan Omar’s home here in DC. We stand with Representative Omar in the face of this political persecution. Whatever “Border Czar” Tom Homan says, we know that Representative Omar is being targeted for consistently championing working-class demands such as Medicare for All, Abolishing ICE, a Green New Deal, and an Arms Embargo on Apartheid Israel. The October 12th raid marks an alarming escalation in the Trump administration’s attacks on our democratic rights, following earlier attacks on activists like Mahmoud Khalil and the Prairieland defendants. The repressive powers of the imperial presidency, built on violence against people abroad and at the border, are being turned inwards. Even citizenship offers tenuous protection: a naturalized citizen who dares to oppose Trump faces the ever-growing immigration apparatus and the threat of losing her rights. When an entire class of people is denied rights, fascists will expand that class to encompass all their enemies. Here in DC, where we are denied statehood and subjected to federal occupation, that threat is part of daily life. The same Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) officers who carried out this raid routinely police our streets and kidnap our neighbors, making the attack on Representative Omar part of the broader assault on our city and our right to govern ourselves. To beat back this fascist advance, we must unite our struggles against political repression, for full rights for everyone, regardless of citizenship, and for a Free DC. Only through unity can the working class win the battle for democracy. Free DC! Abolish ICE! Free All Political Prisoners! The post Statement in Solidarity with Ilhan Omar appeared first on .

articles.title: The Problem With Homeownership
articles.author: Michael Ledger-Lomas
articles.content: A few days from now, my adopted hometown of Vancouver in British Columbia is going to elect a new mayor and council. The low turnout in municipal elections here skews toward affluent owners of detached houses who pay the most property tax and grumble about it. Mayor Ken Sim and his ABC (“A Better City”) party, who won the 2022 election, understand their base: they froze property taxes this year after abolishing the living wage for city employees. The ABC administration also implemented a wave of layoffs and promises to repeat the trick next year if reelected. Meanwhile, underfunding has left two-thirds of the city’s community centers to crumble away . Although ABC has given property developers a free hand to put up towers in the city’s core, they have not touched the zoning regulations that prevent the construction of apartments across most of Vancouver, which interwar planners intended to be a suburban city of detached homes. Sim’s party has also stoked the dread of the transient poor that has always thrived in its more chichi neighborhoods by imposing a ban on new supportive housing and hiking the police department’s inflated budget. Although ABC’s progressive opponents have condemned these actions as cruel, many of them are no keener to challenge homeowners by permitting greater density. Vancouver is but one example of the property-value politics now widespread across Canada, in which the desires of existing homeowners take precedence over economic development or the common good. The historian Joshua Specht suggests that such politics are even more pronounced in the United States. Property Values: The Rise and Fall of the American Homeowner asks how and why municipal officials, planners, and politicians decided to take the side of homeowners against real and imagined threats to the value of their investment. It emphasizes the accidental triumph as well as the social costs of a narrow cult of private ownership that took off because it promised to maintain moral and political principles dear to Americans. Property and Ownership Specht comes to this project as a discerning analyst of market failure. Red Meat Republic , his first book, explained the rise of nationwide cattle markets that turned later nineteenth century Americans into insatiable consumers of beef. It also showed how poorly efforts to manipulate those markets often worked out: cattle ranchers lost their shirts to meatpackers, while country towns that remade themselves to handle livestock traffic failed when it migrated to better-connected locations. The foundations of the American home, Specht argues, turn out to be no less shaky. It takes Specht half of his book to get to houses. “The American story is the story of land,” he argues at some length, before presenting the cult of homeownership as the most striking of its subplots. The founding fathers dreamed of a Roman republic of independent farmers whose sturdy labor would make a patch of the new world their own and confer on them the independence that theorists insisted was crucial for participation in politics. This dream was a nightmare for indigenous peoples. Although historians now celebrate their intermittently effective resistance to settler aggression, they were displaced from their lands and eventually confined to reservations. Nevertheless, the yearning for land of one’s own certainly popularized democratic ideals among settlers. Specht tells the story of the rebel tenant farmers of New York State, who rose up in the 1840s against the old stock landowners who had tightened the screws on them. Disguised as the Native Americans they had replaced, in a loaded allusion to the Boston Tea Party, they hazed their rent collectors and disputed their leases. The moral economy of the crowd — some said mob — emboldened them to demand the right to own the land that their toils had improved. Although their ringleader, “Big Thunder,” was jailed, they prevailed, not least because New York State’s political parties sensed electoral advantage in courting them. Slavery is often regarded as the original sin that poisoned and then nearly broke up the United States, but Specht argues that these controversies came second to the primal question of who should own the soil. John Brown and his godly terrorists killed farmers at Pottawatomie Creek in Kansas because they had arrived there from slaveholder states. “Free soilers” like Brown wanted to ensure that this newly created territory belonged to independent proprietors rather than being snapped up by the South’s satanic aristocracy. After the Civil War began, the North tried to end the Southern plantocracy for good. The Emancipation Proclamation would rob it of its workforce, while the rollout of the 1862 Homestead Act in the West would establish America as an egalitarian democracy of small farmers. That vision still required wiping indigenous people off the map. Brown’s bloodstained creek bore the name of the Potawatomi people who had been marched there from Indiana before settlers pushed them still further west. General William Tecumseh Sherman of the Union Army pivoted from burning plantations to starving indigenous societies into submission by killing their buffalo and destroying their crops. A landowning democracy never took off in the defeated Confederacy. Sherman wanted to carve smallholdings out of plantations for the “respectable Negroes” who had flocked to his army. But President Andrew Johnson was a white supremacist with no desire to create a black yeomanry. Northern elites accepted the planter argument that only their large-scale estates — now worked by dependent, though nominally free, laborers — could produce enough cotton to feed northern mills. The Southern Homestead Act (1866) was the best Washington could do for black Southerners: it allocated them plots on federal lands, but these were too poor to make viable farms. In 1900, three-quarters of black farmers in the South were still tenants. Hopes of colorblind landownership nonetheless took a good while to fade. Specht points to the black homesteaders who trekked to Kansas to found Nicodemus, a boomtown that soon supported two newspapers. Landowning Democracy in a World of Finite Land Nicodemus shrank once it became clear that no railway would run near it. Western homesteaders soon learned that their towns could only survive if the farmers they hosted could get their produce to market. Yet the only way to build railways was to offer enormous land grants to railway companies. Because railways could redraw their routes at almost any time, they had an edge speculating in property, enriching themselves and stranding others. Land became a commodity rather than a firm basis for a continental polity. An agrarian republic also had to reckon with an unstable climate. The rush to homestead the West after the Civil War coincided with a wet period that encouraged the tilling and grazing of its soils. This changed when droughts and locust plagues set in. The steam-powered integration of farmers into far-flung markets also proved to be a curse after distressed Argentinians dumped their wheat in the United States and crashed prices. A landowning democracy presupposed a limitless supplies of western land. But as the historian Frederick Jackson Turner first observed, the consolidation of California and the completion of railways to the Pacific had closed the frontier. The fear grew that a grasping minority could now monopolize a finite resource at the expense of small producers. This explained social reformer Henry George’s abstruse but popular proposals to tax the value of land. It also motivated the populism of William Jennings Bryan, who urged the adoption of bimetallism to loosen up the currency and so to inflate away the debts of mortgaged farmers. Although Bryan won the Democratic presidential nomination in 1896, his populism turned out not to be that popular outside the rural South and Midwest, because it had little to say to the growing number of Americans who worked in cities. Where did America’s future lie, if not with farmers? Before Specht turns to the rise of the homeowner, he points to an important false start: the vision of Jane Addams, a wealthy woman who pursued the gospel of social reform in Chicago. She experimented with running a farm and went to Russia to commune with the novelist and ascetic Count Leo Tolstoy. Back in her adopted home of Chicago, she decided that she did not want to be an urban peasant who baked her own bread and instead helped cofound Hull House, a social hub that promoted the mixing of classes and ethnicities. Chicago was America’s future: a place that reflected the country’s heterogeneity and compensated for it by encouraging the “Americanization” of its residents. The second half of Property Values explains why this urban “social democracy” never materialized. The main cause was the state’s resolute defense and then eager promotion of private homeownership. It began as a panicked response to the mounting problems of agriculture, which became a crisis after the Great Depression. Farmers had borrowed heavily during the 1920s in order to industrialize their operations. They were then hit hard when American banks and foreign lenders sought to contract their lending and interest rates rose. The return of drought and the erosion of topsoil in the West compounded the crisis. The banks foreclosed on people and sold off farms, bringing about the first nationwide drop in home prices with the onset of the Great Depression. America’s “Resettlement” This essentially rural crisis evoked an emotional defense of homeownership from successive presidents. In 1931, Herbert Hoover observed that it “makes for happier married life” and so for “better citizenship.” He felt that “homeowners no matter how humble they may be” were the mainstays of “liberty and freedom.” Franklin Delano Roosevelt spent heavily on such phrases, passing the Emergency Farm Mortgage Act to bring relief to troubled farmers and creating the Home Owners’ Loan Corporation. In its first three years, it refinanced one million home loans on the kind of terms that are still familiar: amortization over the course of the term at fixed rates of interest. By 1936, 10 percent of all non-farm mortgages were managed by the corporation. Congress also created the Federal Housing Administration (FHA), which insured mortgages, and the Federal Savings and Loan Insurance Corporation, which insured deposits in savings and loan associations. Roosevelt’s New Dealers spoke of a “resettlement of America” that moved the site of ownership to the suburbs. Farmers would be subsidized to end overproduction of crops and the rural population would shrink. The future lay with wage earners toiling in factories and offices to pay off mortgages. Men would make the payments and women would make homes with the aid of new labor-saving gadgets. They would live outside the “skyscrapers and tenements of New York and Chicago”: homemaking required grassy yards in which adults could relax and children play. These priorities tied housing to the automobile and so to the burning of gasoline, with huge consequences for the built environment and the climate. Specht, however, is more interested in what they did to sharpen social and racial inequalities. The FHA’s decision to refuse loans to homebuyers in black or racially mixed areas ruled out a genuinely egalitarian democracy. Redlined districts subsided into slums because black homeowners could not borrow against their homes to renovate them; houses in these neighborhoods perversely became more expensive as builders had no incentive to increase supply. To the indignation of black organizations, William Levitt and other postwar suburban developers used racially restrictive covenants to obstruct non-white buyers. Residents who bought into their developments accepted the premise that black neighbors would harm their investment. When Bill and Daisy Myers bought a house in the Philadelphia suburb of Levittown in 1957, they endured a violent campaign of harassment before finally moving away after five years. Homeowner Representation Without Taxation For Specht, this ugly episode was more than an explosion of atavistic bigotry. It was a response to how markets operated: residents were likely correct to fear that racial mixing would depress prices in Levittown. Of course, this was not a result of a natural economic law — it was the result of the real estate market structurally organized by developers and financial institutions to set a higher price on ethnically homogenous neighborhoods. Even Quaker activists who supported the Myers urged the need to temper the “flow of negroes” into Levittown. Many protesters were consistent in their own minds in claiming to approve of the “nice” Myers while vitriolically opposing them as neighbors. Specht’s materialist reading of racism perhaps underplays the visceral character of the reaction to the Myerses: the people who waved Confederate flags and burned crosses on lawns worried about miscegenation as well as mortgages. A few stood against this immoral economy of the crowd. The Wechslers, who lived next door to the Myers, braved antisemitic threats for standing by them. Yet in 2000 over 90 percent of Levittown was still white. American homeowners today — even in fiercely liberal districts — continue to mobilize against renters, immigrants, or other undesirables who threaten the value of their homes. In addition to their fellow citizens, many homeowners came to view the state as a threat, forgetting that federal backing made the mortgage market viable to begin with. Specht illustrates this with a brisk telling of the rebellion against property taxes that shook late 1970s California. Investors seeking a hedge against inflation had poured money into homes. Prices rose across the nation but rocketed in Los Angeles County, where the impossibility of everyone living in a roomy detached house by the beach, or even near centers of employment, engineered an artificial scarcity of housing. Because tax assessments were computed as a fraction of the market value of homes and revised to take account of the sales price of comparable properties, bills soared accordingly. Homeowners remained more or less quiescent only because pliable and sometimes corrupt assessors were willing to keep assessments artificially low. When this element of discretion vanished, the result was a rabble-rousing campaign to pass Proposition 13, which capped the property tax rate at 1 percent of assessed value and restricted annual increases in assessed value to 2 percent. The Californian rebels resembled the Levittown racists in securing their own market position to the exclusion of other moral or social considerations. They were not wrong to resent the fact that property taxes in California were 50 percent higher than the national average. Yet the passage of Proposition 13 in 1978 did enormous damage to the funding of public goods — and of schools in particular — for decades to come. By limiting the annual increases in the assessed value of existing owners’ homes, it privileged incumbents over newcomers, shielding the former from the impact of subsequent increases in house prices. New entrants to the Californian market were stung by taxes assessed on the high prices they had just paid. An effort by one purchaser, Stephanie Nordlinger, to challenge this unfairness in the courts failed in 1992. Specht wryly notes that she still owns that home and so has long since benefited from the injustice she once contested. The revolt had big ideological ramifications nationwide, putting Americans on guard against “wasteful government.” Ronald Reagan, governor of California while the revolt gathered steam, took this resentment of taxation with him to the White House. The spread of homeowner associations as a vehicle for property development in recent decades has further entrenched selfishness as a governing principle: homeowners who pay high fees to have their associations fix their private roads and collect their trash now wonder why they must also pay property taxes to the city. The BANANA Republic The last chapter and epilogue of Property Values show how the 2008 crash pushed the treatment of homes as tradable assets to its disastrous finale. Its origins lay in the rise of mortgage-backed securities, which expanded the amount of capital available to lenders. They issued more and more loans with small down payments, high loan-to-value ratios, and teaser rates that initially kept monthly payments low before resetting. Yet bundling mortgages into securities and dividing them into different “tranches” — ostensibly safe claims were sold to investors while toxic residual risk spread throughout the financial system — disguised how risky such practices were. Foreign banks eager for a share of America’s growth were happy to purchase these securities. The sums poured into housing doubled the price of the average home, encouraging speculative buyers to flip homes for profit. Existing homeowners refinanced, extracting trillions of dollars of equity from their properties to finance renovations or just to buy consumer durables. The inability of “subprime” borrowers to keep up with their repayments finally caused the banks to initiate a wave of foreclosures. This tanked values in boomtowns like Las Vegas: buyers who now owed much more than their waning assets were worth often abandoned or vandalized their homes, perpetuating the downturn. The federal government proved keener to rescue the financial institutions that had made this market than homeowners. President Barack Obama shrank from “cramdown” legislation that would have shrunk the liabilities of individual borrowers. He also had to reckon with a fierce revival of prejudice over which Americans deserved to own homes. Many on the Right blamed the crisis on ill-considered loans to ethnic minority homeowners. The Tea Party movement arose amid ferocious opposition to government mortgage relief for struggling borrowers. Prices have rallied since the crash, not least because homeowners in the most sought-after and dynamic parts of the United States have blocked further development near them. NIMBYs (Not in My Backyard) of coastal California have hardened into BANANAs (Build Absolutely Nothing Anywhere Near Anyone), protecting home values not through naked class or racial prejudice but by posing as guardians of the environment. A tenuous but malign stability has therefore settled over the American housing market. Around two-thirds of Americans still own homes, but with the average price roughly double its 2010 level, new owners are often carrying grotesquely higher levels of debt. It is not just price pressures but a deranged climate that is hollowing out this lopsided homeowner democracy. Global warming is supercharging Californian wildfires and tropical storms in Florida, forcing states to prop up housing markets as insurers of last resort. Urban Abundance or the End of Ownership? Property Values is a model of the academic trade book. It is as fluent as it is gloomy. Each of its chapters reads like a superior kind of New Yorker essay, starting with a person or a community whose heroism or sufferings illustrate a circuitous but inexorable drift toward disaster. These horrible histories of the present often suggest that life in North America could have turned out differently — fairer, nicer, less polluting — if only we had listened to this or that visionary. But can Specht offer us a way out of the housing trap whose jaws so slowly closed around us? Not really. He respects the continued popularity of homeownership and so won’t give up on it. He shares the conviction that owners maintain their homes and so take pride in their communities more than renters do. With the frontier long closed, where to find a new “abundance” of places for Americans to own? Instead of sprawl, Specht urges “density”: filling in the costlier metropoles with higher complexes (and perhaps smaller homes) as well as expanding cheaper cities so that almost everyone can own a row house or a condo. He also offers some diffuse suggestions for cultivating “egalitarianism without exclusion” that Jane Addams would have approved, such as going for neighborhood walks or putting on potluck suppers. These are reasonable proposals but do not explain how we might overcome the entrenched suspicion of the property developers that would be required to construct enough urban condos for sale in some version of a free market. Here in Vancouver, for instance, such sentiment is just as common among renters who fear “demoviction” and professional planners who prioritize “deep urbanism” over speedy construction as it is among boomers ensconced in multimillion-dollar heritage houses. Specht’s emphasis on cities also comes as a plot twist, given how abruptly his story of ownership jumps from farms to suburbs. It is hard to see how federal or state agencies could be pushed to give up subsidizing the lives of suburban car drivers. The same holds true here in Canada, where provincial governments spend on highways but too often won’t fund the urban and intercity transit infrastructure that cities need to grow. Specht never considers whether we should abandon or heavily qualify the dream of ownership that has bent North American life out of shape — and has never been feasible for many people with low or irregular incomes. Ownership could sustain community rather than encourage selfish fear of outsiders, but it usually hasn’t; housing markets could offer dignity and security to the majority, but in the end they haven’t. There is a reason why social democrats across Europe and North America once focused on building urban nonmarket housing for rent. Access to health-giving and dignified housing without regard to income was meant to be the material foundation for the kind of ethical community dear to Jane Addams. Specht vividly illustrates the moral and political dangers of confusing property values with public values. Might it not be time to separate them once again? articles.title: Western Thought Justified Animal Cruelty
articles.author: Ondine Sherman
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. At age seven, sitting at the dinner table with my family, I prodded my fork into a thick, squishy brown shape on my plate. My grandmother, who lived with us, had cooked her traditional Lithuanian-Jewish Litvak meal, and everyone had dug in. “ What is it? ” I asked. My beloved gran whispered back from across the table, “tongue.” I stuck out my tongue. “ This kind? ” She smiled. “ Yes, darling, but from a cow, not a little girl .” It was my first moral shock. Animals are our friends, aren’t they? Certainly, my dog Bronnie was, and all the animals in the picture books and animated films I saw as a child suggested this. Do we cut out our friends’ tongues and eat them? My second moral shock came years later when I saw images of the horror of industrialized animal agriculture and factory farms. How can grown-ups allow this? What I didn’t know then was that some of the most influential thinkers in Western history had already answered these strange paradoxes. The answers to these questions, and Western society’s broad agreement, have led to the systemic violence resulting in animal cruelty we see today, which I have spent my life trying to fight. Our toxic relationship with animals has existed for more than 2,500 years. And while it may feel like humanity has advanced and we are progressive, we have inherited an ancient school of thought that normalized animal suffering and integrated it into our social structures; it is the water we swim in today. Around 88 billion land animals were slaughtered globally in 2024. Meanwhile, people catch trillions of fish each year . These figures show a huge surge in meat consumption since reporting systems were established in 1960. Sentient Media reported that “poultry consumption has skyrocketed over the last 60 years: between 1961 and 2022, [as] the average person went from eating 2.86 kg of chicken every year to 16.96 kg—an increase of almost 600 percent.” Despite decades of animal protection advocacy, suffering keeps growing. Sentient (feeling) animals are subjected to what many consider torturous lives: impregnated, separated from their young, caged, mutilated, and killed daily. Their suffering is not only legal but also unremarkable, part of the systemized functioning of our industries, institutions, and daily meals. Animals are legally classified as property , and many governments do not consider them sentient or as having inherent moral value. They are objects under our control. Scholar Lori Gruen distinguishes between two kinds of anthropocentrism , or human-centered thinking. One is inevitable, given our human vantage point. The other kind, which she terms arrogant anthropocentrism , rests on the claim that humans are superior to all other beings. It is this belief in human superiority that justifies animal exploitation and is the focus of this article. We begin by asking, where did this idea come from? Humans have eaten animals and used them for labor for time immemorial. This was supported by several ancient influencers and thinkers, almost all of whom were European men, who sanctified their use in the Western worldview. This moral permission structure has been carved into the bones of our laws, institutions, pedagogies, and civil societies. Philosophy didn’t invent our use of animals, but it justified and normalized that use. Sociologist Pierre Bourdieu, whose work reflected views similar to those of French sociologist Émile Durkheim, believed that human life is deeply social and that we each inherit ways of thinking from the culture and society we are part of. Bourdieu said , “In each of us, in varying proportions, there is part of yesterday’s man; it is yesterday’s man who inevitably predominates in us, since the present amounts to little compared with the long past in the course of which we were formed and from which we result.” Ancient Foundations Scholars tracing the historical origins of the ideas that shaped our treatment of animals often arrive at the same starting point: the ancient Greeks. Their rationality and reasoning provided the human-animal hierarchy with its philosophical backbone. Plato imparted his teachings to Aristotle, and their ideas accumulated into a tradition that became foundational and ingrained in every aspect of life. Plato argued that rational men possessed immortal, superior souls, while enslaved people and barbarians lacked the capacity or strength for reasoning, and animals had inferior souls driven by desire and emotions. This theory shaped the rationale behind our worldview and was used to determine the moral worth of humans and nonhumans. Today, we can recognize this hierarchical thinking as the kind of overlapping inequality examined through an intersectional lens , which Merriam-Webster describes as “the complex, cumulative way in which the effects of multiple forms of discrimination (such as racism, sexism, and classism) combine, overlap, or intersect especially in the experiences of marginalized individuals or groups.” Aristotle reinforced this hierarchy. He argued for virtue ethics : Every living being has a characteristic nature and a capacity to flourish in accordance with that nature. For instance, humans have reason, and so flourishing means justice and contemplation. Based on Aristotle’s theory, rationality measures moral worth, and the world is accordingly structured in a hierarchy. Plants exist for animals, and animals exist for humans. He said , “Since nature does nothing purposeless or in vain, it is undeniably true that she has made all animals for the sake of man.” Finally, the Stoics, despite their positive legacy in promoting equality among men, primarily maintained a doctrine that elevated human fraternity while denying animals ethical consideration. Pointing to the works of Aristotle and the Stoic doctrine of oikeiōsis , which states that “human beings share a kinship with other humans but not with other species of inferior intellectual endowments,” the journal Arhe states that in the 21st century the doctrine of “human exceptionalism” is used “to justify the wholesale slaughter worldwide of non-human animals for food, clothing, medical and entertainment purposes.” Alongside the Greek philosophical tradition, monotheistic religions conferred divine authority on hierarchical systems. The word “ dominion ” in Genesis has been understood, for centuries, as a social license for humans to use animals for their benefit. Monotheistic religions also broadly denied animals a soul, placing them squarely outside the circle of moral concern. The Church Fathers cemented this into institutional doctrine. St. Augustine was one of the most influential theologians and philosophers in Christian history, and he argued that animals existed for human use . He is credited with first cementing the interpretation of dominion as part of Church doctrine through scripture. Centuries later, St. Thomas Aquinas linked Aristotle’s hierarchy directly to scripture, helping embed it in Catholic doctrine. Aquinas, however, cautioned that one must be kind to animals, not because they have inherent moral value, but because cruelty to animals makes us harsher to one another. However, dissent existed within the religious tradition, with certain voices challenging orthodoxy. For example, in the 12th and 13th centuries, the mystic St. Francis of Assisi preached reverence for all creation and urged people to treat animals as kin rather than property. He was later named the patron saint of animals and the environment. However, sadly, Francis was an exception. Pope Pius IX, in the 19th century, reaffirmed what had been an institutional doctrine for over a millennium: We have no duties toward animals. I first discovered the theological debate about animals many years ago when I read Richard Schwartz’s Judaism and Vegetarianism . Exploring current scholarship, I have come to understand that the meaning of the word “dominion” in Genesis, and even its translation, is hotly contested. Some theologians argue that humans’ God-given role was intended to be stewards, a duty to care for creation rather than a license to exploit it. However, historically, the dominion interpretation became ingrained in Western law, science, and culture. On the consequences of this view, Bible Odyssey, a biblical scholarship resource, points to “the abuses that notion has seemed to lead to in the modern period.” It adds that “Human activity is a key factor in the currently galloping rate of species extinction. The factory farming of animals and fish is a major driver of environmental degradation in North America and, increasingly, around the world.” Scientific Revolution and Enlightenment René Descartes further entrenched animals’ low societal status in scientific thought. Animals, in his view, were automata , unfeeling machines. In his framework, kicking a dog was no different from kicking a clock. This justified the expansion of vivisection practices (live experimentation on animals) because if animals cannot suffer in any morally relevant sense, it does not matter what we do to them. Descartes’s influence was not merely academic; it shaped laboratory practice and legal frameworks whose legacies remain. The Enlightenment promised liberation and reason. For animals, the news was less liberating. Baruch Spinoza both disagreed with Descartes’s claim that animals were mindless and famously rejected religious authority (and was duly excommunicated by the Amsterdam Jewish community for it). However, his views on animals were more conservative. While he accepted that animals feel, he concluded it didn’t matter. He wrote that those who cared that animals were slaughtered were led by “ womanish pity .” In his view, pity is irrational, a feeling rather than a thought, and therefore beneath serious philosophy. He concluded , “[W]e are… permitted to… use [the lower animals] at our pleasure, and treat them as is most convenient for us.” Immanuel Kant’s exclusion of animals from moral consideration has had great and lasting influence. For Kant, the capacity to represent oneself as an “I,” that is, to be a self-conscious, rational subject, is what gives a being moral worth. Animals, lacking this, are things. “All animals exist only as a means, and not for their own sakes,” he wrote in his Lectures on Ethics . “We have no direct duties to animals.” Kant also drew on the Book of Genesis to justify human authority over nature, forging a direct link between the religious tradition I explored earlier and Enlightenment philosophy. Echoing Aquinas, he argued that we should avoid cruelty to animals not for their sake but because it might lead us to treat each other badly. Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel brought this tradition to a kind of culmination. For Hegel, full consciousness —or the capacity for self-awareness, reflection, and shaping one’s place in history—marks what it means to be truly human. In his theory, animals are trapped in the present, driven by instinct, and incapable of the self-determination that generates moral standing. Humans are therefore naturally superior. (By the 19th century, this dismissal of animals having moral worth had acquired a clinical label: zoophil-psychosis , applied to women activists deemed “obsessively” sensitive to animal suffering, their concern dismissed as nervous and overly tenderhearted. The term is no longer used, but the contempt lingers in other phrases such as “crazy cat lady.”) Even as anthropocentrism is taken for granted today as simply the way things are, and eating animals is considered natural, necessary, and normal , we can trace articulations of this hierarchy and entitlement back to a handful of European men. Without the long tradition of dominant Western philosophical thought, from Plato and Aristotle through Descartes and Kant, our relationship with animals may have looked entirely different. Those Who Argued Back Despite what many scholars consider the prevailing orthodoxy of a Western anti-animal worldview, a long and rich history of heterodox voices dates back to the sixth century BCE. These thinkers held an unusual worldview and, in some cases, a diet that rejected animal products. They questioned and abandoned the view of animals as separate or lesser; rather, they argued that animals have inherent value and moral worth and deserve equality and rights. These philosophers defended animals on the grounds of sentience, kinship, and compassion. For example, Pythagoras, considered one of the first recorded ethical vegetarians, claimed that humans have no innate superiority over other animals. The Cynics argued that happiness came from living according to nature rather than convention, and Diogenes famously held up dogs as models of the simple, unselfconscious life humans should aspire to. In the Roman era, Plutarch posited that animals were rational and sentient, possessed virtues that humans lack, and deserved justice. His treatise On the Intelligence of Animals is arguably the first major philosophical work to argue that animals possess judgment, memory, and language. He wrote : “But for the sake of some little mouthful of flesh, we deprive a soul of the sun and light, and of that proportion of life and time it had been born into the world to enjoy.” Two centuries later, Porphyry went further, arguing that justice should extend to animals. In On Abstinence From Animal Food , he approvingly quoted the earlier philosopher Dicaearchus, who wrote that “together with the slaughter of animals, war and injustice were introduced.” Later, in the 16th century, French philosopher Michel de Montaigne argued that our own processes of understanding are limited , and that animals may possess forms of reason and sociality that we are simply unable to perceive. During the Enlightenment, David Hume argued that animals do have thought and reason, and a generation later, Arthur Schopenhauer formed an elaborate ethics of sameness: Compassion, he argued, is the only true foundation of morality, and it cannot stop at the species line. “The assumption that animals are without rights and the illusion that our treatment of them has no moral significance is a positively outrageous example of Western crudity and barbarity. Universal compassion is the only guarantee of morality,” Schopenhauer wrote in On the Basis of Morality . Meanwhile, much of contemporary animal advocacy draws on Jeremy Bentham’s famous utilitarian formulation : It is not “Can they reason?” but “Can they suffer?” These thinkers did not necessarily win their argument in their own time. But they kept the question alive: Do animal lives matter? Other Ways of Knowing These histories of philosophical thought were primarily written by European men and filtered through the lens of those who defined what constituted knowledge. These ideologies conveniently left out the vast diversity of human cultures that never adopted the human-animal binary in the first place, and offered a radically different vision of the human-animal relationship. Through this article, I hope to provide brief insights into the richness of these diverse traditions. Many Indigenous cosmologies are grounded in kinship with animals rather than dominion over them. Anthropologist Deborah Bird Rose described many Indigenous Australian understandings of Country as a living community of people, animals, plants, waters, and ancestral beings, where relationships of care and responsibility sustain life, and where Country is home. Rather than a human/animal division, the world is understood as full of persons, only some of whom are human, who live in partnership with each other. As the late Yolngu ceremonial elder David Gulpilil once observed : “We are brothers and sisters of the world. Doesn’t matter if you’re bird, snake, fish, kangaroo: One Red Blood .” In Mi’kmaq culture , in what is now Canada, animals are considered siblings, beings on the same spiritual and physical continuum as humans. In Haudenosaunee and Anishinaabe traditions , ecosystems are understood as societies with ethical structures and interspecies treaties, and animals are active members who directly influence how humans organize themselves. “The Euro-Christian imagination firmly divides nature from culture and associates human beings and animals according to this binary logic. Animals are assumed not to possess culture or reason or morality or language. This is not true for Indigenous knowledge systems,” states the journal Religions published by MDPI. Ecofeminist philosopher Val Plumwood observed that while Western thinking sets humans apart from nature, many Indigenous traditions conceive of animals, plants, and humans as sharing a common life force with continuity and fluidity between all life. As Potawatomi philosopher Kyle Whyte writes , “Kinship refers to qualities of the relationships we have with others—whether others are humans, plants, animals, fishes, insects, rocks, waterways, or forests.” In this worldview, the line dividing humans from animals does not exist, and what matters is the quality of relationships and their reciprocity. Together, these perspectives suggest that arrogant anthropocentrism was—and is—not inevitable. Rethinking Our Relationship With Animals The suffering of trillions of animals stems from ideas developed over centuries, embedded in law, language, and institutions, and passed on so thoroughly that most of us have never thought to question them. It is a sea of speciesism , in which animals are assigned lower or no moral worth solely based on their species membership. But a counter-tradition has always existed. And something is shifting. A growing body of scholarship in critical animal studies , multispecies justice , and ecofeminist thought is actively challenging our anthropocentric foundations. And the animal movement is growing and becoming more mainstream . For example, legal personhood cases for animals are being argued in court, and the animal agriculture industries are investing in plant-based food tech. “With this increased exposure to posthumanist critiques of the legal system and its status for and treatment of animals, an increasing number of those involved in legal education are rethinking the law’s species-based hierarchy that places humans at the apex. This flourishing interest in animal law is paralleled by growth in the field of Critical Animal Studies (CAS),” stated an article in Animal Law Review . Even our grammar is slowly changing. As Potawatomi botanist Robin Wall Kimmerer has observed , the language we use shapes how we relate to the living world. For example, many animal advocates, myself included, do not use the term “it” to refer to an animal . But much remains to be done to undo the injustices of the past. After more than 180 years of organized animal advocacy, many of the systems that exploit animals remain firmly in place. Lasting change will require developing new moral frameworks—frameworks that ensure our treatment of other animals aligns with fundamental principles of justice, equality, and rights while also respecting, revering, and caring for relationships with all beings, human and otherwise, allowing us all to flourish. Ideas can be deconstructed, and unjust systems can be rebuilt. The historical origins of the ideas that shape the human-animal relationship remind us that they are not fixed or inevitable, but rather assumptions shaped by cultural and philosophical traditions we have chosen to accept. We can discard these learned patterns that taught us to see animals as resources or property and instead rebuild a relationship based on interdependence and kinship. As a seven-year-old at the dinner table, I didn’t understand how my friends could be considered food or treated so cruelly. Now I know it was the water we were swimming in. The history traced here reminds us that this water was neither natural nor inevitable, but shaped by ideas that became embedded in our institutions and everyday lives. And because those ideas were created, we can question them, too. This article was produced by Earth | Food | Life , a project of the Independent Media Institute.

articles.title: Active Membership Achieves Key Goals in New Local 613 Contract
articles.content: UE Local 613 ratified a new four-year agreement on September 14, achieving key goals set by the local entering into negotiations. The union, which consists of the teachers, speech language pathologists, registered nurses, and therapists who work at the Western Pennsylvania School for Blind Children, ran a strong contract campaign rooted in active member involvement. All members will be guaranteed an immediate minimum increase of at least $5,000 in the first year of the new agreement, with an average increase in year one of over $10,000. Step one on the most widely used scale will increase in year one from $48,568 to $58,000, with the top step on the same scale increasing from $98,620 to $109,750 in the first year. Significant improvements were gained on every step of each scale, with substantial increases on every step in each subsequent year of the contract. “The gains we achieved on salaries will allow our extremely deserving members to pay their bills, meet their basic needs, improve the living standards for themselves and their families, and try to keep up with economic demands,” said UE Local 613 President Alison Oniboni , who also served as co-chair of the bargaining committee. “So much of our campaign was rooted in the message of increasing our compensation so that the school can better recruit and retain employees. With this agreement, not only do our current and future members benefit, but ultimately the students and community we serve. There is no better feeling to know that the gains made at the bargaining table will allow us to provide better continuity of service, which is what our students need to receive the education and healthcare services they deserve.” Colleen Benton , the other co-chair of the bargaining committee, added, “It was very rewarding and inspiring serving on the bargaining committee. The group worked tirelessly to fight for the contract we achieved. Our membership stuck together and without a doubt, that helped give us the momentum we needed to reach the kind of agreement we ultimately did.” One of the local’s key goals on compensation was to shorten the salary scale, thus shortening the time it takes members to reach the top of their scale. The new contract will see an immediate decrease in the number of steps on each salary scale from 24 to 20. “Reducing the number of steps on our salary scales will not only lead to better pay for our members, but will result in more equitable compensation based on seniority," said Benton. In other wins, there will now be a $2 per hour shift differential for second- and third-shift nurses and a new $4,000 yearly stipend for orientation and mobility specialists. The number of paid bereavement days for loss of an immediate family member will increase from three to five. Registration fees for attendance at professional conferences will now be paid by the employer and meal allowances for attending those professional conferences will increase from $60 to $80 per day. The Induction Mentorship Program stipend will increase from $1,000 to $2,000, and the New Employee Mentorship Program stipend will increase from $1,000 to $1,500. The contract will now include a $250 stipend for in-house staff presentations at the school. The local also kept the increases to employee premiums for enrollment in the EPO insurance plan minimal. In another major victory, the local won full incorporation of the newly organized occupational therapists, physical therapists, certified occupational therapy assistants, and physical therapy assistants into the contract. “I am so proud of my co-workers for trusting each other in taking the step to unionize and join UE Local 613,” said enthusiastic bargaining committee member and occupational therapist Hannah Pecyna . “We already see the difference having a union makes — having a voice on the job means having a true influence on your working conditions and, in turn, the learning conditions of our students. Nobody knows our jobs and how to best serve the students more than the staff working directly with the them every day.” “What makes this local so special is how democratically it is run and how involved and active we were throughout negotiations,” added bargaining committee member and physical therapist Diane Campbell . “Speaking on behalf of the therapists, we are really excited to be part of the union and help build the local together. Us joining the union has been a long time coming and it is a good feeling to be part of something bigger.” The local’s contract support committee distributed surveys throughout the campaign to help identify areas of importance to the local, and the negotiating committee provided regular updates to members during bargaining. These updates included impromptu gatherings at the school amongst the membership. Members collectively wore their union shirts in solidarity on Mondays during negotiations. “The school definitely saw the local as a united and strong force” said bargaining committee member Patrice Bucheli . “In retrospect, the contract campaign really kind of started when the therapists were organized into our union earlier this year. The fact that we joined hand in hand made us that much more powerful as a group throughout the bargaining process.” The rank and file emphasized working conditions as a core priority entering into negotiations. In turn, the contract will now have caseload language establishing workload targets for speech language pathologists, occupational therapists, and physical therapists. Language will be added allowing missed duty-free time to be restored and used in the future, the number of flexible scheduling days for teachers and nurses will increase from 10 to 12 each year, and the local maintained its 45-minute preparation periods that will now be guaranteed to therapists. In another major win, the contract will include a new retiree health insurance stipend of $500 for every year of service to be available for continuation of coverage upon retirement. The stipend will be available for any member with 20 or more years of service. “The gains made on retiree healthcare mean a lot,” said bargaining committee member Kim Snair . "The work we do as direct care providers is physical and takes a toll on the body. Having the option to retire a little earlier and have continuation of coverage will have a hugely positive impact on some of our longest-serving members. "While it was not everything we wanted, the retiree stipend is both a win and a stepping stone upon which future contracts can build.” The union also fought back concessionary proposals that would have allowed the school to mandate working additional days, extend probationary periods, utilize temporary employees for longer periods of time, and significantly limit the amount of parking spots members would have long-term. “We met with the school at the bargaining table over twenty times, and as a committee dozens of other times preparing for negotiations,” said bargaining committee member Jackie Demoise . “The resiliency of the committee was incredible. We were resolute in our conviction that our members needed and demanded something significantly different and better, and stuck to that objective. We were not to be moved off our fundamental beliefs during many long nights at and away from the bargaining table. We would not have achieved what we did if not for our positive attitude and a healthy degree of stubbornness.” “When reflecting, it was truly a labor of love to serve on a committee like this and for a local like this,” summarized Oniboni. “I think that’s how we all felt, that’s why we succeeded like we did. Our membership supported the bargaining committee fighting at the negotiating table. I am grateful for all of the help we received from our contract support team. We had everyone united and working towards a common purpose. That’s what it’s all about,” The UE Local 613 bargaining committee consisted of President and Co-Chairperson Alison Oniboni, Co-Chairperson Colleen Benton, Kim Snair, Patrice Bucheli, Hannah Pecyna, Diane Campbell, and Jackie Demoise.
