articles.title: War on the International Criminal Court
articles.author: Lawrence S. Wittner
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. On October 9, only hours after the announcement of the award of the Nobel Peace Prize to Navi Pillay, a former judge on the International Criminal Court (ICC), the Trump administration imposed its latest sanctions on the global judicial body. According to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, “we will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate.” When the ICC became operational in 2002, it represented a major breakthrough for the human rights groups that had campaigned for it. The new organization had the mandate to prosecute individuals for genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and, after 2018, the crime of aggression. Once nations ratified the ICC’s authorizing document, the Rome Statute, they took responsibility for arresting these individuals and submitting them to the Court for trial. Designed to complement, rather than to replace, national criminal justice systems, the ICC could prosecute cases only when countries were unwilling or unable to do so. A total of 125 countries ?nearly two-thirds of the world’s nations?have ratified the Rome Statute. Since its founding, the ICC (headquartered in The Hague, the Netherlands) has acted to hold individual perpetrators accountable for the world’s gravest atrocities. Its actions included opening 34 cases (some with more than one suspect), holding 17 different investigations across four continents , issuing 61 arrest warrants, and, thus far, issuing 13 convictions and 4 acquittals . From its inception, however, U.S. officials were wary of the ICC. In the United States, President Bill Clinton signed the Rome Statute, but refused to present it to the U.S. Senate for ratification, warning that it had “significant flaws,” including the inability to “protect U.S. officials.” His successor, George W. Bush , “unsigned” the treaty in 2002 and signed U.S. legislation authorizing military force to liberate any American nationals it held for crimes. During Trump’s first term as President, he denounced the ICC before the UN General Assembly and imposed economic sanctions and visa restrictions on top ICC officials for any effort to investigate the behavior of U.S. personnel in Afghanistan. Russian officials, too, soon realized that enforcement of international law threatened them. Although, initially, the Russian government signed the Rome Statute and participated constructively in the ICC, it withdrew its signature after Ukraine appealed to the ICC in 2014 and 2015 to investigate Russian war crimes in Ukraine. The ICC did initiate a preliminary inquiry that, after the full-scale Russian invasion of 2022 and Russia’s murder of Ukrainian civilians and prisoners of war in Bucha, expanded into a formal investigation. In 2023, the ICC issued arrest warrants for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Commissioner for Children’s Rights Maria Lvova-Belova for the kidnapping of thousands of Ukrainian children. Related: How Trump’s Labor Policies Are Cutting Worker Pay Denying any wrongdoing in Bucha , the Russian government also dismissed the charge of kidnapping as “outrageous.” Dmitry Medvedev , deputy chair of the Russian Security Council, threatened a Russian hypersonic missile attack upon the ICC headquarters. Meanwhile, the assault on the ICC escalated. Although U.S. President Joseph Biden scrapped Trump’s sanctions on the Court and authorized sharing information with it during investigations of Russian atrocities in Ukraine, he and numerous officials of other nations denounced the ICC’s November 2024 war crimes arrest warrant for top Israeli officials. Netanyahu assailed what he called “the antisemitic decision” of the ICC and said that Israel refused to comply with it. With Trump’s re-election, the campaign to destroy the ICC went into high gear . In February 2025, he imposed sanctions on the ICC prosecutor. That August, Secretary of State Marco Rubio , labeling the Court “a national security threat,” added ICC judges to the sanctions list. In late 2025, a top Trump administration official told Reuters that there was “growing concern” that “the ICC will turn its attention to the president, to the vice president, to the secretary of war and others, and pursue prosecutions against them.” That was “unacceptable, and we will not allow it to happen.” The ICC, he said, had been informed that, unless it amended its founding document to ensure that it would not investigate the Republican president and his top officials, new, very punishing U.S. sanctions would be imposed on the Court. The Russian government also ramped up its attack . In December 2025, a Russian court, retaliating for the ICC’s arrest warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova, convicted the ICC prosecutor and eight ICC judges, in absentia, of “unlawful prosecution,” sentencing them to terms of imprisonment ranging from 3-1/2 to 15 years. In July 2026, Rubio announced what the U.S. State Department called “a sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court to U.S. sovereignty.” It would “feature a whole-of-government response to systematically disable the ICC’s ability to operate” and destroy the Court “brick by brick.” That August, imposing additional sanctions on Court officials , Rubio proclaimed “our unwavering mission to protect Americans from this sham of a court.” Meanwhile, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called on Latin American and Caribbean governments to sever their ties with the ICC. Related: Trump’s Canada Crisis Shows How Fragile Alliances Really Are Many observers, of course, were appalled by the Trump administration’s behavior. The European Union immediately expressed its backing for the ICC, while Germany’s Foreign Minister declared that the Court made the world “safer and more just.” In a biting article, Kenneth Roth , a former executive director of Human Rights Watch, argued that “the administration’s real goal is to secure impunity for war crimes.” Nevertheless, the campaign against the ICC is having a serious impact. In late July, thanks to U.S. government pressure , Venezuela and Chad announced their withdrawal from the Court’s Rome Statute. The number of withdrawals now stands at five , including Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger. The latter three are ruled by military juntas allied with Russia. As the Nobel committee warned when announcing the Peace Prize, the “judges and institutions of international law are under political attack.” If the attack succeeds, it will produce a disaster not only for the rule of law, but for the cause of human rights.

articles.title: FDR, Trump, and Fascism
articles.author: Walter G. Moss
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. According to the English newspaper The Guardian , in the late summer of 2026, “Donald Trump . . . declared himself to be the ‘greatest’ US president ever.” Some others have proclaimed him the greatest of our lifetime. My own assessment— shared by many presidential experts? The worst president of my octogenarian life. Take just one comparison, that with FDR, President Franklin D. Roosevelt. According to a review of historian William I. Hitchcock’s new book, A Shadow Over the World: Franklin D. Roosevelt, the Rise of Fascism, and the Making of America’s World War II , “ the indelible feature of Roosevelt’s Presidency was his desire to protect democratic norms and processes amid crises, even as critics accused him of being a power-mad dictator or a Communist sympathizer.” In 1936, he proclaimed that “here in America we are waging a great and successful war. . . . It is a war for the survival of democracy. We are fighting to save a great and precious form of government for ourselves and for the world.” Hitchcock declares that this was “the thesis of the rest of his presidency.” Rather than protecting our “democratic norms,” Trump seems determined to tear them down. To take just one example, consider Trump’s recent ban of White House access for ‌journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico. And lest one thinks that FDR had no challenges to such norms, Hitchcock reminds us of “Americans’ embrace of eugenics and racism, anti-egalitarianism and antisemitism, nativism and illiberal politics,” and “the literal Fascism that took root in the U.S. during the thirties, when avowedly pro-Nazi organizations held mass rallies at Madison Square Garden and Henry Ford cozied up to Hitler.” Hitchcock adds that “during the thirties, anti-Communism was at least as powerful as antifascism in the U.S.” Related: Why Affirmative Action Needs to Continue One presidential scholar, Robert Dallek, commented that he wrote his biography of FDR “to remind people, especially a younger generation with limited knowledge of American history, of what great presidential leadership looks like.” Although both Hitchcock and Dallek admit that FDR had his flaws and faults—e.g, policies toward Jews, immigrants, and Nazi Germany—they think, as Dallek writes, that “neither Congress nor public opinion was as liberal or progressive as the president, and FDR often chose not to be too confrontational, which would have lessened his popular appeal.” And regarding “Roosevelt’s options in dealing with Stalin” in WW2, Dallek adds that they “were severely limited by political and geographical realities.” Dallek also had some thoughts about President Trump. In an earlier HNN interview he noted that he was “thinking of writing a book about democracy’s demagogues,” including “Huey Long and Father Coughlin [both often mentioned in his FDR biography], Joe McCarthy, George Wallace, and probably a closing chapter on Donald Trump, because I think he fits the pattern of these past demagogues.” In a December 2017 Newsweek essay Dallek stated that “it is clear Trump is unfit to serve,” and lawmakers should “invoke the 25th Amendment” to remove him from office.” In contrast to FDR, as Dallek observed, Trump sounds more like the “past demagogues” the scholar has mentioned—Long, Coughlin, Joe McCarthy, etc. In 1935, after Roosevelt proposed a “wealth tax,” William Randolph Hearst, whose papers and magazines circulated among millions of Americans, denounced it (sounding like the later McCarthy) as a “soak-the-successful” measure that was “essentially Communism.” And in 1944, running against Roosevelt for president, the Republican candidate Thomas Dewey charged that FDR’s New Deal was “Communist inspired.” Dallek also noted that among FDR’s “New Deal’s fiercest critics were many wealthy businessmen.” For example, the head of General Motors said, “with unemployment insurance no one would work; with old-age and survivors insurance no one would save; the result would be moral decay, financial bankruptcy and the collapse of the republic.” Billionaires are also among Trump’s supporters, and this should not surprise us since he is one and they (and he and his family) benefit the most from his policies . But capitalism before FDR was not especially favorable toward the working class, and Dallek observes that, like the progressives before him, he took “giant steps in humanizing the American industrial system.” Related: Obama, Trump and the Battle Over American Values Another difference between FDR and Trump is the people they surround themselves with, including those they bring into the government. One Trump critic has noted that in his second term, what is demanded is “complete loyalty to Trump.” FDR, however, surrounded himself with differing voices, including progressive ones (e.g., Interior Secretary Harold Ickes, Labor Secretary Frances Perkins, and his wife, Eleanor Roosevelt), as well as those more cautious. In summary, one can do no better than quote The Atlantic’s Jonathan Rauch , who after resisting the label “fascist” for Trump during his first term, concluded after a year into his second one: “Over Trump’s past year, what originally looked like an effort to make the government his personal plaything has drifted distinctly toward doctrinal and operational fascism.”

articles.title: Student Protests Are Making Their Mark on Serbia’s Election
articles.author: Lela Vujanić
articles.content: Sitting in the trashy garden of a café frequented by students near an iconic Belgrade market, we are, naturally, discussing the elections. A somewhat hippieish father of a friend complains that the situation is terrible, that he’s never seen such polarization, and that decades-old colleagues are barely on speaking terms. He tells me he tried to lighten the atmosphere, joking “Guys, I am neutral, you can relax, you can all be yourselves with me.” His remark didn’t sit well with either camp. Nobody in Serbia these days seems to like “neutrals,” though it seems that this despised group could decide the outcome of the October 25 parliamentary elections. There is an electric mood in the country. There have already been irregularities and sporadic individual acts of violence against opponents by members of the ruling party, with more widely expected before the vote. Previous police violence against protesters and the alleged use of a sonic weapon during a March 2025 demonstration are still vivid in the collective memory. The latter has even become the subject of Lawrence Abu Hamdan’s fifteen-channel video installation currently exhibited in Venice. Few expect election day to pass peacefully. Aleksandar Vučić — competing to become prime minister, to which end he recently stepped down as president — is mainly communicating to his nominally “progressive” party’s (the Serbian Progressive Party, or SNS) own base, trying to harden its core vote and prevent defections. Student protesters, who registered as a group of citizens under the name “Student List–Students Win,” are campaigning under the slogan “Serbia or Mafia,” pointing out corruption, para-police gangs, and connections between the state and organized crime. They’re trying to capture all the neutral and still-undecided voters, those lacking information or interpretations of what’s going on, as well as past abstainers. There’s a fight for every vote, including those in the diaspora who will now have to be stubborn to get their votes counted: due to the authorities’ controversial decision, some will have to vote in the middle of the night or even fly thousands of miles to cast a ballot, if they can afford it. These elections come in the twenty-fourth month of “pumping it up,” as the students’ popular slogan calls it. The vote takes place a few days ahead of the second anniversary of the collapse of the Novi Sad railway station canopy that killed sixteen people and triggered a massive wave of student blockades and protests as well as local mobilizations through people’s assemblies, known as zborovi . In between, we have seen historic blockades and protests, assemblies and organizing , mass politicization and emancipation. Many lives were put on hold, many suffered government repression, including arrests and job losses, and many invested their labors not only in elections but in building structures meant to survive them. But now the elections are served on the table, and, as the occasion demands, we need to look at the challenger, the incumbent, and the ever-so-precarious election forecasts. The Electoral Experiment Called Student List The Student List, consisting of 250 candidates, was finally revealed to the public in mid-September, after the elections were formally called. The criteria for the list were set by student assemblies ( plenums , in Serbian) from faculties across the country; no students were to be on the list, to show their dedication not to power but to the common good; no opposition party officials, to show a break with oppositional politics as usual that yielded no results; no prior members of the ruling coalition; and proven support for the student movement and its program. There are a few household names, from a famous basketball player to an actor to a farmer who fiercely resisted the Rio Tinto lithium project. But in general, the final list features “ordinary people,” meaning that most Serbians will not recognize these names or what politics they represent. All candidates went through an unprecedented multistage process in which faculties could propose candidates and challenge one another’s nominations. Many candidates were vetoed for different (sometimes rather bizarre) reasons, among them the playwright Maja Pelević, who stays committed to the movement. “The veto process was a litmus test, ensuring that this was genuinely a shared, democratic decision of all the faculties,” she says, emphasizing that the plenums , not individual influence or name recognition, had the final say. This list is meant to represent the population in general, though its success in that regard is mixed. The gender split is 55.6 percent men and 44.4 percent women. Geographically, 75 percent of candidates come from four cities that are university centers. Most striking is the occupational structure — more than 50 percent of the candidates are from the education sector, from high school to university professors. For comparison, education accounts for less than 10 percent of Serbia’s total registered employment. Part of the reason is the support that educators gave students, meaning they also suffered government repression most. Candidates do not belong to the same ideological or political factions, and some take pride in being politically nonaligned. The impression is that this was by design. It is unknown who would take ministerial or cabinet roles in case of victory, how such a diverse group of candidates could find political and programmatic harmony in parliament, or who would prevent those elected from acting contrary to the students’ program. It is worth pausing now, for both me writing this text and for you reading it; if all of this sounds wild and experimental, that is because it is. Though there are historical reference points, like the construction of Poland’s Solidarność electoral list, the experimental and unprecedented character of the Student Lists, vetoed and voted for by anonymous assemblies representing the mass movement, is being used by opponents to discourage people from voting. We hear fearmongering that “salaries and pensions could be put in question” and that “the country could fall into chaos.” The (Un)importance of Having a Program The electoral program, developed in an equally long and thorough process of collective deliberation between plenums , labor collectives, and sectoral associations, is not fully revealed yet. The rather brief version presented as Student Plan focuses on cleaning up the state — primarily the judiciary — and the media; general claims of reforming education and health care; and providing accessible housing for youth (no luck for tenants of my age group, it seems); though fighting import monopolies and permanent employment after twelve months of temporary contract are also part of the plan. The vagueness of the program’s eleven points seems to bother no one, confirming that both students and protesting citizens are primarily focused on replacing the current government, and that the competing economic or cultural frames are postponed for after the elections. The incumbent’s offer, meanwhile, rests on the stabilitocracy of macroeconomic indicators, foreign direct investment (FDI), and economic maneuvering between foreign powers, which also includes close cooperation with Israel . In domestic policy, Vučić has, throughout the years, repeatedly positioned himself as a protector of lower-income strata. Actually, this is how he got in power in 2012 in the first place, following the waves of rampant privatization and job losses, as part of transitional “shock therapy” implemented in Serbia a decade later than in the rest of the East. But not only was Vučić no clean newcomer, but in practice the privatization and deregulation of the labor market continued, while the public sector was clientelistically tied to the ruling party and its needs. The incumbent is still playing these cards, trying to depict students and their supporters as out-of-touch with economic realities and as instruments of the West, while he himself is a patriotic protector of the nation, an economic tiger (as the SNS slogan has it) and almost an anti-imperialist smooth operator, successfully fighting external and internal dragons. While the Student List candidates are mainly talking about abstract freedom and the less abstract questions (if not first on everyone’s mind) of corruption and institutional order, some on the Student List are determined to center labor. Živojin Milovanović, candidate number 31, and a machine technician at the Electric Power of Serbia, says: “[in] agency employment, commonly known as ‘daughter companies’ in Serbia . . . workers are modern-day slaves, and I will keep repeating that. They do the hardest possible jobs, yet are paid far less than their colleagues, work on temporary and short-term contracts, and have no real voice.” As an early member of the Social Front, an alliance of students, workers, and farmers that emerged within the student movement, he promises changes to the labor code and the laws on strike action that would guarantee people’s right to organize in trade unions and ensure that they face no consequences for going on strike. “The regime shaped the laws to serve its own interests. It took control of the trade unions, turning them into its obedient servants. They did not fight for workers; instead, they suppressed every form of workers’ struggle, leaving workers without protection and without any means to change anything. The Students’ List wants to change all of this.” For proposals like these, the Party of the Radical Left (PRL) has offered the Student List “critical support,” arguing that despite the limitations of its still-incomplete program, it includes candidates and positions worth supporting. It is likewise maintaining pressure for a broader anti-capitalist agenda. Forecasting Into the Void Much has been debated about creating a referendum-like atmosphere, with Vučić versus the students as the key contenders. Credible and independent polling is scarce. In the latest election forecast from mid-September by Faktor Plus, the Vučić-led coalition list was at 48.6 percent, while the Student List, in continuous growth according to their previous polling, stood at 37.1 percent. Earlier polling by other organizations (CRTA and NSPM) showed the Student List ahead, by 44.9 to 44.4 percent. Across pollsters, about a quarter of voters are yet to make up their minds. There is a consistent expectation of high turnout, likely above the 58.8 percent recorded in 2023. While Vučić and his SNS are employing arena rallies, TV ads and appearances, and an army of bots on social media, the students are relying on messaging groups and social media, plastering the city with stickers, and, more importantly, making their presence felt in person: cycling across Serbia, organizing public rallies and events, and covering multiple city locations in a single day. Pelević, who is a member of a local, Belgrade-based popular assembly, helps students with campaigning in her municipality. “Door-to-door is essentially another form of decentralized organizing. We’re not politicians. We’re neighbors ( komšije in Serbian), we’re students, and we go out and talk to people about the problems that affect both them and us. So the way we have these conversations is completely different from when some politician comes knocking on your door, has no idea what your problems are, and pretends they’re going to solve them.” Election After-Party High expected turnout and a sizable bloc of undecideds are main factors cited as decisive in regard to the election result; but it may also be that the SNS camp will face defection. Economic slowdown, inflation and the limits of FDI as a core strategy for growth, visible in the depletion of workers’ rights and dignity as well as degradation of the environment, could break the spell of Vučić’s “protection.” The students and their candidates have exposed the regime’s corruption and the havoc in Serbia’s institutions. What still needs doing is to tie these questions to an economic agenda: first, by showing that Vučić’s political authoritarianism and economic neoliberalism work hand in hand; second, by making clear that getting rid of one without the other will not be enough. After the elections, the economic contradictions of a landlocked country whose place in the global economy rests heavily on cheap labor and lithium reserves will remain. The mass democratic opening created by the movement could also slip into parliamentary politics as usual. What happens next will depend on the movement’s ability to rebuild and sustain its power beyond the ballot box, through people like Milovanović and Pelević and the practices they represent. And ultimately, the election may be one step on a historical path that depends not only on local conditions but also on future international alliances. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: trumps american history
articles.author: Eva Amar
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. I have a confession to make, and I'm not particularly proud of it. Somewhere between middle school and high school, I decided history wasn't for me. It seemed like an endless parade of dates, timelines, and wars, interrupted by still more wars. I paid enough attention to pass the tests, but I certainly wasn't sitting on the edge of my seat waiting to find out what happened next. What did any of that have to do with my life? Well, seventy years of living have given me a rather different perspective. History isn't simply a collection of dates, wars, and presidents. It's our baseline. Without it, how can we recognize the warning signs of something we've already lived through? This year America celebrates its 250th birthday. Compared with civilizations whose histories stretch back thousands of years, we're practically adolescents. We've packed extraordinary wrongdoing into those two and a half centuries, but we've also advanced science, medicine, education, and human rights, helped defeat tyranny abroad, and produced generations willing to challenge injustice at home. We have much to celebrate. And much to answer for. We began by taking land from the people who were already here. Native Americans were displaced through conquest, broken treaties, forced removals, and massacres. We declared that all men were created equal while allowing human beings to be bought and sold as property. Related: He said. He said. End of Story. Then came the Mexican–American War of 1846–1848, which ended with Mexico losing approximately 55 percent of its territory. California, where I live, was once part of Mexico, along with much of the Southwest. Which brings to mind something Mexican Americans have been saying for generations: “We didn't cross the border. The border crossed us.” For some families, their ancestors lived here before the border moved. We abolished slavery but subjected Black Americans to generations of segregation. We denied women the vote, excluded Chinese immigrants by law, and permitted forced sterilization under eugenics programs. In 1939, the United States turned away the St. Louis, carrying 937 passengers, most of them Jewish refugees fleeing Nazi persecution. The passengers returned to Europe, where several countries accepted them; ultimately, 254 were murdered in the Holocaust. Only three years later, our government began incarcerating approximately 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry, most of them American citizens. During the McCarthy era, accusations of communist sympathies could amount to professional and social death sentences, destroying careers and reputations on little more than suspicion. Our government surveilled civil rights leaders, including Martin Luther King Jr., while gay Americans endured generations of discrimination. Yet Americans also fought to correct injustices. The Civil Rights Act became law in 1964. Marriage equality became the law of the land in 2015. And in 2022, the Supreme Court overturned nearly fifty years of constitutional protection for a woman's right to decide whether to terminate a pregnancy she cannot, for whatever reason, carry to term. I'm not asking anyone to inherit the guilt of previous generations. I'm asking us to inherit their lessons. Facts Are Stubborn Things In 1770, John Adams, defending British soldiers accused in the Boston Massacre, reminded a courtroom that “facts are stubborn things.” More than 250 years later, those words deserve another hearing. On January 29, 2025, the president signed Ending Radical Indoctrination in K–12 Schooling. The executive order directs federal agencies to develop strategies addressing what it calls indoctrination, including through federal funding, and reestablishes the President's Advisory 1776 Commission. The administration says it wants patriotic education, parental rights, and an end to teaching children that they are personally responsible for historical injustices. Children shouldn't carry the guilt of previous generations. But there's a difference between assigning blame for slavery and teaching children how slavery worked, whom it harmed, and why Americans fought to end it. The order does not itself ban teaching slavery or segregation. But its definitions and funding provisions raise the question of whether teachers may feel discouraged from examining uncomfortable history honestly. On March 27, 2025, the president signed a second order: Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History. This one extends to the Smithsonian and federal historical sites, directing officials to address presentations the administration considers divisive or improperly disparaging. The administration says it is restoring accuracy and celebrating American achievement. Historians and preservation advocates worry about political influence over what the public is allowed to see. At the President's House in Philadelphia, which served as the presidential residence for George Washington and John Adams before the White House was built in Washington, D.C., the National Park Service removed exhibits documenting the lives of people enslaved by Washington in January 2026. Philadelphia sued, and a federal appeals court subsequently cleared the way for the administration to replace the original displays. Washington helped establish a republic dedicated to liberty, and he enslaved human beings. Both are true. Why should knowing one require concealing the other? And what about the Smithsonian, where generations have gone to discover their country's story? Should the exhibits change according to what each administration finds flattering? History isn't a public relations campaign. Nor should the free press become one: its job is to examine the record, not repeat an administration's preferred version. It's optics. Pure optics. The Lessons We Keep Encountering History doesn't stay neatly tucked away in textbooks or museum exhibits. It has a way of rearing its head in the morning news, sometimes in ways that are uncomfortably familiar. Take immigration, for example. Undocumented immigrants harvest our food, clean our hotels, care for our elderly, and build our homes. Many have raised American-born children. According to the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, undocumented immigrants paid an estimated $96.7 billion in federal, state, and local taxes in 2022, including $25.7 billion toward Social Security and $6.4 billion toward Medicare. A country has the right to enforce its immigration laws. But surely there's a distinction between someone who poses a genuine danger and someone whose principal violation is entering without authorization or overstaying a visa. Instead, we're seeing immigration operations involving officers with covered faces, sometimes without visible identifying information. Questions about detention conditions, oversight, and the use of force deserve answers. And then there are the children. Related: Stay Woke: What My Father Learned About Race in America A child waiting outside school for a mother who never arrives. A little boy watching the clock, wondering why his father hasn't come home from work. Many children affected by immigration enforcement are American citizens. They have broken no law, yet may suffer devastating consequences when a parent is detained. The St. Louis and the Japanese American families forced from their homes belong to different historical circumstances. But isn't recognizing both the differences and the unsettling echoes part of why we study history? And Then There Is the Rest of the World And history doesn't stop at our borders. It follows us into the relationships we've built with other nations, the promises we've made, and the alliances we've come to depend upon. For generations, America helped build alliances with Canada, Britain, France, Germany, and other democracies. We stood beside them through wars and crises, and they stood beside us. After September 11, 2001, NATO invoked Article 5, its collective-defense provision, for the first and only time in its history. It was invoked in defense of the United States. Now some of our closest allies are preparing to rely less on us. They haven't abandoned America, but they're building arrangements that may no longer depend on our participation. Then there are questions about our own use of military force. In September 2025, the United States military attacked a boat in the Caribbean suspected of carrying drug traffickers. Two men survived the first strike and clung to the wreckage. A second strike killed them. The administration defended the operation as lawful. But whatever those men were suspected of doing, suspicion is not conviction. They were clinging to the wreckage when the second strike came. For generations, ours was a country others often turned to for help. We weren't always right, and we never accomplished those things alone. But now I wonder who will be there to pick us up if we fall. The People on the Beam There's a famous 1932 photograph of eleven construction workers eating lunch on a steel beam suspended hundreds of feet above Manhattan. Their feet dangle over the city. They smoke, talk, and eat as though sitting on a park bench. Now imagine that photograph with a different cast of characters: a grandmother clutching her grandchild, a father holding an infant, teenagers, working mothers, retirees. Ordinary Americans, sitting together with no visible safety net beneath them. I'm there, too, seventy years old, wondering whether the institutions we've depended upon will withstand the strain being placed upon them. I've come to believe anyone running for political office ought to be required to pass an eighth-grade government test. I realize there might be a few constitutional problems with that requirement. And considering how little attention I paid in history class, it's quite a concession coming from me. If I could have a do-over in life—and believe me, there are quite a few things I'd like to do over—I'd pay a whole lot more attention to history. At least I had the opportunity to learn it, to ask questions, and to make up my own mind. What happens to children who grow up knowing only the chapters someone has decided are suitable for them? I don't want children taught to be ashamed of America. I want them to know what makes it worth celebrating, what we've gotten terribly wrong, and how much courage it has sometimes taken to make things right. The good, the bad, and the ugly. We don't teach history to tell children what to think. We teach it so they'll have the knowledge to think for themselves. I've spent seventy years witnessing history, much of it without fully appreciating what I was seeing. But there's something else I've come to understand: We aren't simply witnessing history. We're making it. I don't know about you, but I can't look down anymore. And I can't look away, either. Because when good people remain silent in the face of what is happening around them, eventually we're all going down.

articles.title: How Charles Manson Became a Hero of the American Far Right
articles.author: Claudia Verhoeven
articles.content: The person most responsible for the recognition of Charles Manson as a quasi-icon of the twenty-first-century radical right is James Mason. Born in 1952, Mason is a lifelong white supremacist activist who joined George Lincoln Rockwell’s American Nazi Party as a teen, then Joseph Tommasi’s more radical National Socialist Liberation Front, then became even more extreme after he took over that party’s newsletter, Siege (1980–86). He dropped off the radar for two decades following his arrests and incarceration in the 1990s but resurfaced in the 2010s after being “recovered” on the neo-Nazi online forum Iron March, and he is presently acknowledged to be the “grandfather” or “godfather” of white power accelerationism, an ideology convinced that the inevitable collapse of society and subsequent founding of a white ethnostate should be sped up through acts of terrorism. Unlike many others in the white power movement, Mason never concealed his racism or tried to make his extremism more palatable for the mainstream. Whether in his writings or interviews, he is almost obstinately open about his convictions. His 1980s publications particularly make it very plain he hates Jews, blacks, and immigrants and loves Hitler, Rockwell, and Tommasi — plus Charles Manson, “a discovery similar only to the discovery I made when I bumped into Adolf Hitler.” Throughout the 1980s, Mason promoted Manson as a “great leader/philosopher” in Siege , with far-right expert Jeffrey Kaplan going so far as to characterize the newsletter as “primarily a vehicle for the glorification of Charles Manson.” Manson and Mason Siege gained no real traction at the time, but eventually its articles were gathered and bound as SIEGE (1992), a book described by scholars of the far right as “required reading” for contemporary neo-Nazis, “a foundational text — one arguably rivalling even Mein Kampf in contemporary fascist gravitas” and “a neo-Nazi Bible,” held responsible for the spread of online “SIEGE culture” and real-world terrorist networks. Today, therefore, this culture’s celebrated predecessors are Hitler, Tommasi, Mason himself, and Manson. And SIEGE is undoubtedly the key source for understanding the idea of Manson that dominates the far right. But to understand Manson’s own ideas during the years Mason was promoting him, the key source is a far less public one, namely, the astonishing correspondence between the two men. Some years after first finding out about Manson, Mason finally reached out. He initially entered into correspondence with Lynette Fromme and Sandra Good, who were at that time still incarcerated themselves and still very close to Manson. They then made the introductions, and in 1981 Mason sent off an initial letter to Manson. Thus began a correspondence that lasted a decade, maybe longer, and that offers an extraordinary point of access into Manson’s thinking during this period, reveals the extent to which it was Manson who determined the content of Mason’s writing in Siege , and also makes clear where the two men’s respective ideas diverge. As Kathleen Belew has shown, it was broadly during this same period, between 1975 and 1995, that white power consolidated into a new social movement. It was not a resurgence of the Ku Klux Klan but a movement that managed to bring together previously distinct and even mutually exclusive right-wing and racist groups. And crucially, unlike earlier right-wing and racist violence, white power was directed against, rather than in defense of, the state. “The white power movement sought revolution and separation — the founding of a racial utopian nation,” writes Belew, who adds that many in the movement “connected ideas of a radical political future with belief in imminent apocalypse.” The Great Divide The principal catalyst here was the Vietnam War or, rather, veterans who brought the war home, because they were traumatized, because they were inappropriately demobilized and reintegrated, and because they felt betrayed by their own government. White supremacist Louis Beam, for example, who is credited with popularizing “leaderless resistance,” was a veteran who by his own account remained forever stuck in the “rice paddies and skies of Vietnam” and who recognized no difference between the enemy abroad and at home (and at home that enemy did include the state). Many in the movement experienced the 1980s as a downturn, and certainly this was true of Mason. Names known to scholars of the radical right pepper his letters, but Mason’s incessant refrain is that the movement is in dire straits. For the far right, the 1980s felt like far less fertile soil than the early twenty-first century would prove to offer, though even then, during that new century’s first decade, Kaplan could still characterize the movement as “tiny and fractious.” But Belew’s more recent retrospective gaze reveals an upward trajectory and a distinctly new, strident radicalism. “The old ways have failed miserably,” Beam wrote in his 1989 Essays of a Klansman . “Out with the conservatives and in with the radicals! Out with plans for compromise and in with plans for the sword!” At that point, Mason had been railing against conservatism in the movement for about a decade, often in radically antipasséist language influenced by Manson. When Mason first began mentioning Manson to others in the movement, it did not go over well. Though some simply dismissed it — “I’ll consider that this is your latest fantasy and that it’ll be gone in a couple of months” — others fretted: “Now you’ve got me scared,” said one, and another, “Does he plan to become a party member?” But for that very reason, according to Mason, Manson could serve as a kind of litmus test, or “threshold,” something to separate the wheat from the chaff: “Manson represents the great divide between those persons who imagine there still are choices to be made casually on the basis of Establishment mores and those who have a profound, individual sense of ‘no going back.’” Besides, there was the matter of brand recognition and impact: “Charles Manson exerts a fascination over Youth today, in the entire West.” So, undeterred by the fact that movement veterans were nervous about having a notorious murderer and madman join their ranks, Mason continued to promote Manson in Siege : “I have done what I could to inject — subtly and overtly — as many of Manson’s ideas into Movement thought as possible,” he wrote in 1986. Universal Order Indeed he had, and frankly it has not been sufficiently appreciated how extensive was Manson’s influence on Mason, a man whom scholars of the far right have characterized as “one of the most influential ideologues to rethink fascism in the face of twenty-first-century realities.” Comparing the correspondence with the newsletter, it is clear that Manson’s language came to shape Mason’s. Mason really leans into Manson’s discourse of authenticity, for example, so that increasingly enemies inside the movement come to be called “fakers” who are “role-playing” and so on, and Manson himself is identified as the exemplary “Non-Faker.” Very obviously too — and this matters in terms of tracking the movement’s new radicalism — Mason’s modernism came from Manson, a man forever obsessed with being “new” and “now” (or “nuness,” his neologism meaning “no past or place in the past and no thought of future”). “The most important word is NEW! You can’t carry the past into a NEW world,” Manson wrote to Mason. This is also why Manson chides him for any idolatry of Rockwell, or of Hitler for that matter: “If you got no dead heroes, you can be yourself more.” “Your [ sic ] dragging the past on your back,” he warns him, then counsels with the rather Baudelairean “if you’re trying to march Wagner’s music back through with a marching band dressed in 1814 garb you wake up negative thought” and “Fat sloppy people in German dress with armbands on don’t help.” Soon Mason can publish a line about “the entire Right Wing” that might as well have been written by Manson: “If they haven’t been living in 1933, they’ve been living in 1865.” Modernism was also why Manson urged Mason to drop the name National Socialist Liberation Front — “That’s preposterous and it has to go,” he quotes Manson — and adopt instead the name Universal Order. “One world. One government. One mind.” One index finger. Universal Order had a long shelf life. “As we move farther towards the Universal Order, we become more on the offensive with our world view. Wild wishes for the end times,” read a Siege Culture website launched in the 2010s. But according to Nikolas Schreck, Manson had already broken with the Universal Order in the late 1980s, and in retrospect one must wonder about the fact that when Manson recommended the name change, he did also insist that Mason swap out his emblem’s right-facing swastika over an automatic weapon for a left-facing swastika between a set of balancing scales. Kindred Spirits Though in the aftermath of the Tate–LaBianca murders no one on the Right recognized themselves in the Family, in retrospect of course one can see why Manson seemed to Mason a kindred spirit, obviously starting with the swastika, even if it did face the wrong way for a Nazi. There was also Manson’s allergy to miscegenation, including repeat references to the figure of the black rapist and the need to “save” white women and children, both well-worn white racist tropes. To the extent that it meant an imminent, apocalyptic war of the races, “Helter Skelter” must have seemed simply a traditional truism to Mason, who overlooked the fact that Manson and the Family believed that black’s victory over white was karma, and instead focused on promoting the Tate–LaBianca murders as a political attack on the degeneration of a formerly white system. But the crucial element was what Mason imagined Manson’s political project to be: a racial-socialist colony in Death Valley . . . TRIBES of White Warriors, bands of White Men with their Women and Children who have drawn together and then pulled away from the System to allow it to fall without taking them with it. Of course, Mason’s embrace of Manson may have looked mad to more traditional American Nazis in the 1980s, which were after all the heyday of Manson’s most infamous performances on national television, but politically none of this was at odds with the increasingly alienated white power movement. In other respects, however, Charles Manson did not fit well within the white power movement. Manson was never an anti-communist, and to put it mildly, he disliked the (Christian) church. His “Family” was far from nuclear, he promoted free love, and he was neither straight nor cisgender. He and the Family partook in the romanticization of the Old West, imagining themselves as cowboys and Indians and pioneers at Spahn’s and in Death Valley, but unlike white power ideologues, Manson never saw this land as “empty.” And while Manson was a fan of the founding fathers, he was sooner a supporter of Mexican revolutionary Pancho Villa than of the movement-supported Contras in Nicaragua. So even if he was happy to erase the boundaries between war and peace at home, Manson was not a supporter of American empire. Emptying the Zoo Above all, Manson did not overlap with the white power movement on the environment, so that although Mason adopted Manson’s Death Valley–based survivalism, environmental degradation had little to do with it. And this also filtered right into their most basic divergence, which Mason summed up in a 1983 issue of Siege as follows: The Manson people look upon and accept the NS Movement in America with curiosity, some admiration and some dismay. “Hate,” they say, “is not going to get it.” Trying to live in another time and place isn’t going to get it either. To our charges of a monstrous, Jewish conspiracy, they simply counter with the stated belief that people today have a death wish for themselves. We say that without unpolluted, White blood, there’ll be no civilization left. They say that without an unpolluted world, there can be no White Race . . . or any other race for that matter. Indeed, in multiple letters, Manson corrected what he thought was Mason’s understanding of Manson’s views on race or otherwise differentiated those views from Mason’s. Mason’s views are quite straightforward, informed by a white supremacist means-end utilitarianism. Manson’s views, meanwhile, remained contradictory as ever. On the one hand, he continued to believe that races are best maintained rather than mixed and, as of old, recommended that one should only have sex by race: “Only put that rod in something that looks like you,” he writes, and “I’ve only fucked white guys” (though he immediately adds he also “fucked a phony Jew when I didn’t have better sense” and in another letter that he “even fucked a cow once”). But as in the 1960s, he argued that this was as much to preserve other races as it was the white race because, historically, miscegenation had led to the disappearance of people of color. Plus he continued to hold whites in contempt above all others: “There is no white people in the truth,” he writes, and “I get more respect from black brown yellow + red more than I do my own,” or he might snark about “this white pride B.S.” He insists that, from fear of black people, whites use other whites to defend themselves — “You wouldn’t believe the things they have done to me with their fear of black people” — though often, such whites appear in his letters as “PJs” and “PCs,” meaning “phony Jews” and “phony Christians,” that is, categorized along lines of authenticity. He tells Mason that he has a friend who is Jewish, and that he feels “they have a place in this world. The real Jews do.” “Look,” he writes in 1986, “I never ask my people to hate anyone because of race.” In fact, as in the 1960s, Manson’s imagination still settled on a “separate but equal” elite order, but by the 1980s it had hypertrophied, somehow become even more maximalist and militarized. So, whereas James Mason would “send black back” — to Africa presumably — Manson countered with this vision: I would make them the ZZ like the SS only worse (better). The white SS & the Black SS and then do away with the PJs and PCs in the middle. Then I’d put Green back on the land with the air force & army & the navy [&] would empty the zoo & all wildlife back [&] make a garden & only there children could return to earth garden. This is an astonishing rainbow-fascist, eco-totalitarian dream of epic, even biblical, proportions. But it’s not King Charlie ruling a black planet, nor the James Mason–inspired whites-only world promoted by SIEGE culture. Outstripping Manson If initially Manson was too much for Mason’s veterans in the neo-Nazi movement, perhaps ultimately the movement was too much for Manson. Racist and separatist though he was, Manson just never advocated for the elimination of people of color. Aside from the fact that the most important fault lines in his thinking were determined not by race but by what was “real” — and obviously he had no problem with the idea of eliminating an entire world of “phonies” — Manson was also simply too antiwhite. That does not mean that Manson’s letters, at least during the 1980s, were not crammed with racist remarks and antisemitic tropes, because they most certainly were. And in fact, even if part of what the expression “PJs and PCs” captured was whiteness, one suspects that because whiteness was also firmly tied to “money,” the phony/real binary had by the 1980s also become entangled with antisemitism for Manson, though arguably one could read all this as a class-based critique too, because Manson often argued that the powerful used race to keep down the powerless. Finally, for the record: Manson’s interest in Adolf Hitler during the 1960s has been overstated — there exists only the most minimal evidence — but it is impossible to read the letters he wrote to James Mason and come away with anything but the certain knowledge that “AH” was one of Manson’s most prominent discursive tics during that period. Nonetheless, Manson’s views diverge from Mason, neo-Nazism, the far right, and SIEGE culture. It seems important to mark the differences, not least so as to be able to delineate the various strands that make up white radicalism in late modern American culture, and because maybe it matters that in some respects contemporary white supremacism outstrips the extremism of a man whose very face has long been a symbol of the country’s most radical racism. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture.
